# NVIDIA RTX Spark Laptops: What the New Thin, Light Windows Models Mean for You

> **In short:** NVIDIA says its RTX Spark chip now powers thin, light Windows laptops from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, and they are available now. The chip pairs an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX graphics processor with an NVIDIA Grace CPU, and NVIDIA says the systems are built for developers, creators and gamers.

If you have ever shopped for a laptop and seen terms like "GPU" and "CPU" listed without explanation, you are not alone. Here is what NVIDIA's latest announcement actually says, and what it could mean the next time you need a new machine.

## What was announced

NVIDIA announced that laptops based on its RTX Spark platform are now available from six companies: ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. All of them run Windows.

The announcement describes these machines as thin and light, and says they are meant to handle the work that developers (people who write software), creators (people who make photos, videos or music) and gamers do. NVIDIA describes the systems as powerful, but that is the company's own description, not an independent test.

## What is inside

The announcement says the laptops combine two kinds of processing in one "superchip" (a single chip that packs several processors together):

- **A Blackwell RTX GPU.** A GPU is a graphics processor, a chip that is very good at doing many calculations at the same time. That is why it helps with images, video, games and many AI tasks. Blackwell is the name of NVIDIA's chip family.
- **A Grace CPU.** A CPU is the main processor, the part that runs your apps and manages everything else on the machine. Grace is the name of NVIDIA's CPU family.

NVIDIA also says the chip supports up to 128GB of unified memory. Unified memory is one shared pool of memory that both the CPU and the GPU can use, so they do not have to pass data back and forth as much. The "up to" matters: it is the maximum, and the amount on any specific laptop will depend on the model you buy.

## How to read a laptop listing

When you compare laptops, you do not need to understand every chip detail. A few simple checks help:

- **Look at the memory number.** More memory usually means you can keep more apps and browser tabs open at once.
- **Check the processor and graphics names.** Write them down and look them up on the maker's official spec page.
- **Read the claims with care.** Words like "powerful" and "built for everything" describe what the company hopes you will do. They are not measurements.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you mainly browse, email and stream video, the chip details matter less than the screen, battery life and keyboard. Try the laptop in a store before you buy, if you can.
- **For your work or studies**: If your job or school involves video editing, design or coding, look at the memory and graphics specs on the listing, not only the thickness.
- **If you're just getting started**: You do not need to know what a superchip is to buy a good laptop. Start by listing what you do most, then match that list to the spec sheet.
- **If you already use a laptop with a dedicated graphics chip**: Check the maker's support page for updates and driver downloads, which often improve how the graphics chip handles AI and creative software.

The announcement's headline also mentions new models, agent tools (AI programs that can carry out multi-step tasks for you) and games. Those details are not in the material we have confirmed yet, so check NVIDIA's official announcement for specifics before you rely on them.

## Wrap-up

NVIDIA says RTX Spark laptops are now available from six makers and combine a Blackwell RTX GPU and a Grace CPU in one chip, with up to 128GB of unified memory. For most people, the best next step is simple: write down the tasks you do most, then compare the memory, graphics and processor details on the official pages of the laptops you are considering.
